html:
A Roman road built in the 2nd century BCE across the southern Balkans, from Dyrrachium (Durrës) on the Adriatic to Thessalonica and on towards Byzantium. It is named after the proconsul Gnaeus Egnatius, who built it after Macedon became a Roman province in 146 BCE.

It was the eastern half of a great route. Travellers took the Appian Way from Rome to Brundisium, crossed the Adriatic by ship, and then followed the Via Egnatia over the mountains of what is now Albania and North Macedonia, down to Thessalonica and across Thrace.

Armies used it in Rome's civil wars, on the way to Pharsalus and Philippi. Paul the Apostle walked it when he took Christianity to Philippi and Thessalonica.

After Constantinople was founded it became the main land link between the two Roman capitals, and it stayed in use under the Byzantine and Ottoman empires. Stretches of its paving still survive.
